subject: history
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In which month and year did Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicate, paving the way for the Weimar Republic?
questions.explain: The Kaiser abdicated in November 1918 as Germany faced defeat and revolution at the end of the First World War.

questions.q: Which clause of the Treaty of Versailles forced Germany to accept blame for causing the war?
questions.explain: Article 231 required Germany to accept sole responsibility for the war, which many Germans deeply resented.

questions.q: Why did the Weimar Constitution's use of proportional representation contribute to political instability?
options: It produced many small parties, making stable majority governments hard to form
It gave the President no powers at all
It banned all political parties except the Nazis
It prevented anyone from voting until they were 30
questions.explain: Proportional representation led to numerous parties and frequent, fragile coalition governments.

questions.q: The Spartacist uprising of January 1919 was an attempt by which group to seize power?
questions.explain: The Spartacists were left-wing communists, led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, whose Berlin rising was crushed by the Freikorps.

questions.q: Which event most directly triggered the hyperinflation crisis of 1923?
options: The French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr after Germany missed reparations payments
The signing of the Locarno Treaties
Germany joining the League of Nations
questions.explain: The Ruhr occupation prompted passive resistance and the printing of money to pay workers, causing currency to collapse.

questions.q: Which new currency did Gustav Stresemann introduce in late 1923 to end hyperinflation?
questions.explain: Stresemann replaced the worthless mark with the Rentenmark in November 1923 to restore confidence in the currency.

questions.q: What was the main purpose of the Dawes Plan of 1924?
options: To reorganise reparations payments and provide American loans to Germany
To rearm the German army beyond Versailles limits
To abolish the office of President
questions.explain: The Dawes Plan spread reparations more manageably and brought US loans that helped Germany's economy recover.

questions.q: A President rules for a period by issuing decrees that bypass the Reichstag during a crisis. Which part of the Weimar Constitution allowed this?
questions.explain: Article 48 gave the President emergency powers to rule by decree, a provision later exploited to undermine democracy.

questions.q: In which year did Hitler and the Nazis attempt the Munich (Beer Hall) Putsch?
questions.explain: The Munich Putsch of November 1923 was a failed Nazi attempt to seize power in Bavaria.

questions.q: Where did Hitler write 'Mein Kampf' after the failure of the Munich Putsch?
questions.explain: Hitler wrote Mein Kampf while serving a short sentence in Landsberg prison, setting out his political ideas.

questions.q: How did the Wall Street Crash of 1929 help the Nazis gain support?
options: It caused mass unemployment, making extremist parties more appealing to desperate voters
It made Germany wealthy and grateful to Hitler
It forced France to return the Ruhr
questions.explain: US loans were recalled, unemployment soared, and many turned to the Nazis' promises of jobs and strong government.

questions.q: On what date was Hitler appointed Chancellor of Germany?
questions.explain: Hitler was legally appointed Chancellor by President Hindenburg on 30 January 1933.

questions.q: Who was blamed and arrested for starting the Reichstag Fire of February 1933?
questions.explain: Dutch communist Marinus van der Lubbe was caught at the scene, and the Nazis used the fire to attack the Communists.

questions.q: What did the Enabling Act of March 1933 allow Hitler to do?
options: Make laws for four years without the approval of the Reichstag
questions.explain: The Enabling Act gave Hitler dictatorial power to pass laws without the Reichstag, dismantling democracy.

questions.q: In June 1934 Hitler ordered the murder of SA leader Ernst Röhm and other rivals to secure army support and remove threats. What is this event called?
options: The Night of the Long Knives
questions.explain: The Night of the Long Knives eliminated the SA leadership and other opponents, strengthening Hitler's control.

questions.q: Why did Franz von Papen and conservative politicians persuade Hindenburg to make Hitler Chancellor in 1933?
options: They believed they could control and use Hitler for their own ends
They wanted to restore the Weimar Constitution
They were ordered to do so by Britain
questions.explain: Conservatives thought they could restrain Hitler in a coalition, but he quickly outmanoeuvred them.

questions.q: What did the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 do?
options: Stripped German Jews of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews
Guaranteed equal rights for all Germans
questions.explain: The Nuremberg Laws removed Jews' citizenship rights and forbade marriage or relations with 'Aryan' Germans.

questions.q: What was the significance of Kristallnacht in November 1938?
options: It marked a violent escalation of persecution, with Jewish homes, businesses and synagogues attacked
It was a Nazi defeat in an election
questions.explain: Kristallnacht saw widespread state-encouraged violence against Jews, marking a sharp intensification of persecution.

questions.q: A 13-year-old German girl in 1937 is enrolled in a Nazi youth organisation that trains her for motherhood and domestic duties. Which organisation is this?
questions.explain: Girls joined the Bund Deutscher Mädel (BDM), which emphasised health, comradeship and preparation for motherhood.

questions.q: A poster, a controlled radio broadcast and a censored newspaper all glorify Hitler and blame Germany's enemies. Which Nazi minister was responsible for this propaganda?
questions.explain: As Minister of Propaganda, Goebbels controlled the media to spread Nazi ideas and build the Hitler cult.

specSource: Eduqas GCSE History specification; Germany in Transition 1919-39
